references.text: The same expression 'holy convocation' and the prohibition against work are used for the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
The seventh day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread also has a holy convocation and a prohibition against work.
The Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) is described with the same formulations regarding holy convocation and the prohibition against work.
The first day of the seventh month (the Day of Trumpets) has the same commandment for a holy convocation and a prohibition against work.
The eighth day of the Feast of Tabernacles has the same regulations concerning a holy convocation and a prohibition against work.
A parallel text in Numbers describes the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles with a holy convocation and a prohibition against work.
The first commandment regarding a holy convocation and a prohibition against work is given in connection with Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
Deuteronomy describes the seventh day as a solemn assembly for the Lord with a prohibition against work.
The Gospel of John mentions the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles, which is the same feast referred to in Leviticus 23:35.
Jesus speaks on the last, great day of the Feast of Tabernacles, showing the continued significance of the feast in New Testament times.
